title: The End of the Old Gods
objective: After this level you can explain how Christianity and later Islam replaced the old religion.
summary: Christianity spread through Egypt, and the temples closed, the Serapeum in 391 CE and Philae under Justinian. After the Arab conquest of 640 to 642 CE, Egypt became Muslim gradually.

cards.headline: Egypt’s gods outlasted every conqueror. They didn’t outlast a change of faith.
cards.body: The old religion didn’t fall in one battle. It went quiet temple by temple, from the Serapeum in 391 CE to Philae in the 6th century.

cards.headline: A new faith
cards.body: Christianity, tradition says, was brought to Alexandria by St. Mark in the first half of the 1st century CE, and it spread quickly through Egypt. Egypt’s Christians came to be called Copts, and they spoke Coptic, a late form of the Egyptian language. The old tongue lived on. It just had new prayers to say.

cards.headline: The temples close
cards.body: In 391 CE the patriarch of Alexandria and his followers destroyed the city’s Serapeum, the great temple of Serapis, with Emperor Theodosius I’s encouragement, and other temples fell too. One famous holdout was Isis’s temple on the island of Philae, where the last known hieroglyphic inscription was carved in 394 CE. It wasn’t closed until Emperor Justinian’s reign, in the 6th century, and was then made into a church.
cards.callout: Serapeum destroyed 391 CE; Philae closed in the 6th century

cards.headline: Then, slowly, Islam
cards.body: Between 640 and 642 CE, Arab forces under ʿAmr ibn al-ʿĀṣ beat the Byzantine armies and entered Alexandria. Even then, change was slow. Egypt was mostly Christian at the conquest and became Muslim gradually over centuries; historians can’t pin down when Muslims became the majority. By the 12th century the Coptic church itself had adopted Arabic alongside Coptic. Faiths and languages rarely switch overnight.

cards.headline: The end of the old gods: met
learned: Christianity spread through Egypt from Alexandria
The Serapeum was destroyed in 391 CE
Philae’s Isis temple closed under Justinian
After 642 CE, Egypt became Muslim only gradually

questions.prompt: Which temple of Isis kept going until Emperor Justinian’s reign?

options.label: The temple on the island of Philae
The Serapeum at Alexandria
options.rationale: It was destroyed in 391 CE, and it belonged to Serapis.

options.label: The mortuary temple at Medinet Habu
The lighthouse on Pharos island
options.rationale: That was a lighthouse, not a temple.

questions.explanation: Isis’s temple at Philae flourished in Roman times and was not closed until Justinian’s reign.

questions.prompt: Why is it misleading to say Egypt “became Muslim” in 642 CE?

options.label: The Arab armies never reached Alexandria
Egypt was already mostly Muslim before then
options.rationale: It was mostly Christian at the conquest.

options.label: Conversion happened gradually over the following centuries
Egypt went back to the old gods after the conquest
options.rationale: The old temples were already closed.

questions.explanation: Egypt was mostly Christian at the conquest and was Islamized gradually; historians debate when Muslims became the majority.

questions.prompt: Philae’s holdout temple belonged to Isis; from Level 33, what did Isis do in Egypt’s great myth?

options.label: Sailed the Sun through the night

questions.explanation: Isis, Osiris’s wife, sought out and gathered the pieces of his body.
